questions_json.explanation: Babies in the sensorimotor stage (0-2 years) have not yet developed object permanence — the understanding that objects still exist when out of sight. Piaget called this 'out of sight, out of mind.'
options: He has not yet developed object permanence
He is in the preoperational stage
questions_json.q: A 6-month-old baby happily plays with a toy. When his mother hides it under a blanket, he stops looking and plays with something else. What does this show?

questions_json.explanation: Egocentrism — the inability to see things from another person's point of view — is the hallmark of the preoperational stage (ages 2-7). The child assumes everyone sees what she sees.
questions_json.q: A 4-year-old girl covers her eyes with her hands and giggles, 'You can't see me now!' Which preoperational limitation does this show?

questions_json.explanation: The child fails conservation — understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in shape. This is typical of the preoperational stage; children in the concrete operational stage (7-11) pass this task.
questions_json.q: Two glasses hold the same amount of juice. The juice from a short wide glass is poured into a tall thin glass. A 6-year-old insists the tall glass has more juice. Which concept is he missing?

questions_json.explanation: Scaffolding means giving a child just enough support to succeed at a task slightly beyond their independent ability — Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. Support is removed as the child learns.
questions_json.q: A teacher helps a child solve a puzzle by giving small hints instead of the answer. As the child improves, the teacher gives fewer hints. Which Vygotsky concept is this?

questions_json.explanation: This is the secure attachment pattern from Ainsworth's Strange Situation: the child uses the mother as a safe base, is upset at separation, and is comforted at reunion. About 65% of infants show this pattern.
questions_json.q: In a playroom, a 1-year-old explores happily while her mother sits nearby. When the mother leaves, the baby cries. When she returns, the baby reaches out and is quickly comforted. Which attachment style is this?

questions_json.explanation: Authoritative parents set clear rules AND explain reasons, listen, and show warmth. This style is linked to the best outcomes: confident, socially skilled children. It differs from authoritarian (strict, no discussion).
questions_json.q: The Ahmeds set clear bedtime rules for their 8-year-old, but explain why sleep matters and listen to his side. Which Baumrind parenting style is this?

questions_json.explanation: Erikson's stage of identity vs role confusion (ages 12-18) is about forming a stable sense of self. Trying different looks, groups, and beliefs is healthy exploration, not confusion.
questions_json.q: A 15-year-old tries different hairstyles, joins and leaves clubs, and debates career dreams with friends. Which Erikson psychosocial stage is she in?

questions_json.explanation: Adolescent egocentrism creates the imaginary audience — the belief that everyone is watching and judging you. It peaks around ages 13-15 and fades as teens realize others are focused on themselves too.
questions_json.q: A 14-year-old refuses to wear a slightly torn shirt to school, convinced 'everyone will stare at me.' Which adolescent thinking pattern is this?

questions_json.explanation: Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen): as people sense time is limited, they prioritize close, emotionally meaningful relationships over new acquaintances. This is healthy adaptation, not depression.
questions_json.q: A 72-year-old man sees fewer people than before but spends more quality time with his grandchildren and oldest friends. Which aging theory explains this?

questions_json.explanation: Integrity vs despair (65+) is Erikson's final stage: looking back on life with satisfaction brings integrity and wisdom; regret brings despair and bitterness. Life review helps many reach integrity.
questions_json.q: An 80-year-old woman often tells stories of her life and says, 'I have lived well and have no regrets.' Which Erikson stage has she resolved positively?
